variants.title: Run the loop
variants.context: A tool-enabled turn is a controlled loop: the application attaches identity, tenant, state, and only the allowed tools; the model proposes a tool and arguments; code validates schema, permission, scope, risk, confirmation, and budget; trusted code executes with scoped credentials, a deadline, and idempotency; the application returns bounded data or a structured error.
variants.prompt: The model wants to look up an order. Put the loop in order.

items.text: The model chooses a tool and emits arguments claiming to match its schema.
The application returns bounded data or a structured error; the model explains or proposes another call.
Trusted code runs with scoped credentials, a deadline, idempotency controls, and an audit identifier.
Code validates schema, permission, resource scope, risk class, confirmation, and budget.
The application attaches identity, tenant, conversation state, and only the tools allowed for this task.

variants.hint: The model never calls the database itself.
variants.explanation: Each boundary turns probabilistic output into a typed, authorized, observable operation.

variants.context: A tool-enabled turn is a controlled loop: the application attaches identity, tenant, state, and only the allowed tools; the model proposes a tool and arguments; code validates schema, permission, scope, risk, confirmation, and budget; trusted code executes with scoped credentials, a deadline, and idempotency; the application returns bounded data or a structured error.
variants.prompt: The proposal names an order in another tenant. Put the loop in order, showing where it stops.

items.text: Policy checks resource scope and denies the call.
No execution occurs.
The application attached the active tenant.
The model proposed lookup_order with a foreign order ID.
A structured error is returned; the model can explain or ask a question.

variants.hint: Authority is checked before any credential is obtained.
variants.explanation: Schema conformance does not make a request authorized.

variants.title: Run the loop
variants.context: A tool-enabled turn is a controlled loop: the application attaches identity, tenant, state, and only the allowed tools; the model proposes a tool and arguments; code validates schema, permission, scope, risk, confirmation, and budget; trusted code executes with scoped credentials, a deadline, and idempotency; the application returns bounded data or a structured error.
variants.prompt: A write tool is proposed for a high-risk action. Put the loop in order, including confirmation.

items.text: Policy classifies the risk and pauses for user confirmation.
The model proposed the write.
Identity and allowed tools were attached.
The observation is returned to the model as a typed result.
After confirmation, trusted code executes with an idempotency key and deadline.

variants.hint: Confirmation is a policy decision, not a model decision.
variants.explanation: Require confirmation for destructive, expensive, external, or hard-to-reverse actions.

variants.title: Separate the values
variants.context: Keep three values separate: the proposal (what the model requested, preserved exactly), the decision (why policy allowed, denied, or paused it), and the observation (what the tool actually returned or changed). Match results to proposals by call ID, not array position.
variants.prompt: The model’s next turn says the refund “succeeded”, but the tool returned a timeout. Which value must the system trust?
options: The model’s statement, since it summarizes the whole turn accurately.
The proposal, because it records exactly what the refund was meant to do.
The observation the tool actually returned, which here is a timeout.
optionFeedback: Generated prose is not evidence of a side effect in the authoritative system.
The proposal is only what was requested, not what the refund service did.
A timeout is an unknown outcome, and the observation is the only record of it.
variants.hint: Which of the three values is evidence?
variants.explanation: Never replace the observation with the model’s assumption that a call probably succeeded.

variants.title: Separate the values
variants.context: Keep three values separate: the proposal (what the model requested, preserved exactly), the decision (why policy allowed, denied, or paused it), and the observation (what the tool actually returned or changed). Match results to proposals by call ID, not array position.
variants.prompt: Three tools ran in parallel and results are matched by array position. What is the risk?
options: Execution slows down, because position lookups scan the whole result array.
Results can be attached to the wrong proposal once completion order shifts.
There is no risk, since providers return results in the order they were proposed.
optionFeedback: Position lookups are cheap, and speed is not the concern here.
Parallel completion order is not proposal order, so correlate by call ID.
Providers make no such guarantee once calls finish out of order.
variants.explanation: Preserve call IDs across queues, workers, logs, and the next model turn.

variants.title: Separate the values
variants.context: Keep three values separate: the proposal (what the model requested, preserved exactly), the decision (why policy allowed, denied, or paused it), and the observation (what the tool actually returned or changed). Match results to proposals by call ID, not array position.
variants.prompt: Policy denies a call. What should be stored?
options: Nothing, because a denied call produced no side effect worth recording.
Only the model’s explanation of the denial, which reads well in the transcript.
The proposal as made, the decision and its reason, and a denied result record.
optionFeedback: Denials are evidence, and they are the record of what policy stopped.
The model’s prose is a retelling, not the decision record policy produced.
Preserve one result record per call ID, including denied and timed-out calls.
variants.hint: Which values exist even when nothing executed?
variants.explanation: Preserve one result record per call ID, including denied and timed-out calls.

variants.title: Place the check
variants.context: JSON Schema constrains shape; execution policy decides authority. Put identifiers, enums, bounds, and unknown-field rejection in the schema. Keep caller permission, tenant ownership, approval, credentials, budgets, and retry safety in trusted policy code.
variants.prompt: “Does this order belong to the caller’s tenant?” Where does that check belong?
options: In the model prompt, telling it to use only the caller’s own orders.
In trusted policy code, using the caller identity the application holds.
In the JSON Schema, with a required tenantId field on the tool input.
optionFeedback: Prompts are guidance, not authority, and the model can be talked out of them.
Ownership is a business fact that only trusted context can establish.
A required tenantId proves only that a field is present, and the model supplies its value.
variants.hint: Can a schema know who owns an order?
variants.explanation: JSON Schema can constrain shape; it cannot prove business authority.

variants.title: Place the check
variants.context: JSON Schema constrains shape; execution policy decides authority. Put identifiers, enums, bounds, and unknown-field rejection in the schema. Keep caller permission, tenant ownership, approval, credentials, budgets, and retry safety in trusted policy code.
variants.prompt: An argument has a small closed set of values such as summary or shipping_status. Where does that constraint belong?
options: In the schema as an enum.
In policy code.
Nowhere; the model will get it right.
optionFeedback: Closed choices are exactly what enums express.
Shape belongs in the schema.
Hope is not a constraint.
variants.explanation: Make invalid states difficult to express.

variants.title: Place the check
variants.context: JSON Schema constrains shape; execution policy decides authority. Put identifiers, enums, bounds, and unknown-field rejection in the schema. Keep caller permission, tenant ownership, approval, credentials, budgets, and retry safety in trusted policy code.
variants.prompt: The model adds an unexpected field named admin_override. What should happen?
options: Reject unknown fields at the schema boundary where the provider allows it.
Accept it, since extra fields are ignored by the tool implementation anyway.
Pass it through and let the policy layer decide what to do with it later.
optionFeedback: By default JSON Schema allows extra properties, so constrain them deliberately.
A field ignored today becomes a field read tomorrow, and it carries injected intent.
Rejecting at the earliest boundary keeps the field out of every later decision.
variants.hint: What does JSON Schema do with unlisted properties by default?
variants.explanation: Properties are optional unless required, and extra properties are allowed unless constrained.

variants.title: Handle the timeout
variants.context: A timeout means no response arrived before the deadline, not that the operation failed. Read-only calls are safe to repeat; idempotent writes repeat one intent with a stable key; non-idempotent writes need reconciliation before any retry.
variants.prompt: A send_message call timed out. Retry?
options: Yes, because a timeout means the send failed and nothing was delivered.
Yes, exactly once, since a single duplicate message is an acceptable risk.
No. It is a non-idempotent write, so reconcile authoritative state first.
optionFeedback: A timeout is an unknown outcome, and the service may have committed the send.
One retry is still enough to deliver the message twice.
Query authoritative state or route to review before any second attempt.
variants.hint: What could have happened before the deadline?
variants.explanation: Blind retry can create a second message, booking, or payment.

variants.title: Handle the timeout
variants.context: A timeout means no response arrived before the deadline, not that the operation failed. Read-only calls are safe to repeat; idempotent writes repeat one intent with a stable key; non-idempotent writes need reconciliation before any retry.
variants.prompt: A get_weather call timed out. Retry?
options: Yes, within bounds; a repeated read creates no external mutation.
Never, since a repeat may return a different reading and confuse the model.
Only after checking the provider recorded no earlier request.
optionFeedback: Reads are safe to repeat, though they still consume capacity.
A newer reading is expected rather than a hazard, and the call mutates nothing.
There is nothing to reconcile, because a read leaves no external effect.
variants.hint: Does a repeated read change anything?
variants.explanation: Read-only calls still deserve bounded retries.

variants.title: Handle the timeout
variants.context: A timeout means no response arrived before the deadline, not that the operation failed. Read-only calls are safe to repeat; idempotent writes repeat one intent with a stable key; non-idempotent writes need reconciliation before any retry.
variants.prompt: A create_booking call carries a stable idempotency key and timed out. Retry?
options: Yes, with a fresh key so the retry is not rejected as a duplicate.
Yes, with the same key, so the service returns the first outcome.
No, because a write that already timed out must go to manual review.
optionFeedback: A new key is a second intent, so it can create a second booking.
The key makes the retry refer to the same intent.
Review is the answer for non-idempotent writes, and this call carries a key precisely to avoid that.
variants.hint: What does the key do on the service side?
variants.explanation: The service stores the first outcome and returns it for duplicate attempts.

variants.title: Move through the states
variants.context: Every call moves through explicit states: proposed (parse and correlate), decided (validate and authorize), attempted (execute with a deadline and idempotency key), recorded (observe and continue).
variants.prompt: A tool call is processed. Put the states in order.

items.text: Attempted: pass only validated arguments, use least-privilege credentials, attach an idempotency key to supported writes.
Proposed: capture the provider’s call ID, tool name, raw arguments, turn, and task identity; reject malformed or unknown calls.
Decided: apply schema, identity, tenant, permission, approval, budget, and risk checks before obtaining a credential.
Recorded: store status, latency, side-effect ID, and bounded result; return the matching result or error to the model.

variants.hint: Credentials are obtained only after the decision.
variants.explanation: Proposed → decided → attempted → recorded, with durable evidence at each state.

variants.prompt: A call is denied. Put the states it passes through in order.

items.text: No attempt is made.
Recorded: a denied result record is returned to the model.
Decided: denied by policy with a recorded reason.
Proposed and correlated by call ID.

variants.hint: Denied calls still end in the recorded state.

variants.title: Move through the states
variants.context: Every call moves through explicit states: proposed (parse and correlate), decided (validate and authorize), attempted (execute with a deadline and idempotency key), recorded (observe and continue).
variants.prompt: Two calls run in parallel. Put one call’s states in order and note the correlation rule.

items.text: Decided independently.
Recorded and matched back to its proposal by call ID, not position.
Proposed with its own call ID.
Attempted with bounded concurrency and its own deadline.

variants.hint: Parallel execution makes call IDs essential.
variants.explanation: Bound concurrency so one turn cannot exhaust a dependency.
